I am getting on in years, but I have farmed this land in Quzhou since I was a young bride, and I know every corner of it. This year, just like the last thirty years, I will plant the wheat-maize rotation on my 4 mu of land. It is the only sensible thing to do here on the North China Plain — the soil is good for it, the buyers come to the village for both crops, and my nephew helps me with the heavy work. 

For the winter wheat, I will sow around the National Day holiday in early October. I will buy an improved seed variety from the township supply store — I do not remember the exact name on the bag, but it is the one my neighbors say resists lodging and gives a full grain. I will rotary-till the field first to break up the corn stubble, then spread compound fertilizer as the base. I know wheat is hungry, so I will give it plenty of nitrogen: about 20 kg of pure nitrogen per mu, along with phosphorus and potassium. It needs water four times — once before winter to help it settle, once at green-up, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I will spray for weeds once and for insects twice, maybe three times if the aphids are bad. I expect about 1,050 jin... no, kilograms, per mu these days, God willing.

As soon as I cut the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize right away — no time to waste. I will use a hybrid corn seed, one package per mu, and sow it directly without ploughing to save time and labor. Maize does not need as much fertilizer as wheat, but it still needs nitrogen, so I will put down about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate twice, and spray for insects and weeds two or three times total. If the summer rains are good, I should get about 1,100 kg per mu.

I do not try anything fancy. Wheat and maize put food on the table and money in my pocket. That is enough for me.
